title: The Ruthless Pursuit of Above-Ground Living
author: Samuel James
summary: Samuel James continues his 'Reaching the Lost Young Men' series with an essay arguing that young men in crisis need something more specific than a general call to 'get off screens': what he terms 'above-ground living,' a rhythm of productive, embodied life to counter the isolating pull of digital consumption. He opens with the widely reported case of a 14-year-old boy whose suicide followed a parasocial relationship with an AI chatbot, using it to define 'below-ground living' as a mode of existence, not merely a measure of screen time, in which digital substitutes for real friends, work, and identity become normal and even comforting. James argues the antidote is threefold: meaningful work (starting with household chores that give boys a felt sense of agency), genuine friendship (which requires visible absence and real proximity, not virtual community), and confident identity built not on winning but on a theology of failure that removes the fear of trying. He closes with a reading of C.S. Lewis's Screwtape Letters to argue that below-ground living is ultimately a spiritually inert state, neither what we ought to do nor what we actually want, and that recovery is always possible through small, genuine encounters with real joy.
points: James reframes 'below-ground living' as a rhythm of life rather than a screen-time metric, arguing digital withdrawal becomes dangerous specifically when it substitutes virtual relationships for real proximity to family and friends.

He locates the root of many young men's isolation in a felt lack of agency, arguing ordinary responsibilities like chores are what first teach boys the world responds to their effort, making 'above-ground living' feel possible.
He reframes confidence as primarily a product of being unafraid of failure rather than a product of accumulated wins, crediting his own father's non-punitive response to his failures as formative.

He uses the Screwtape Letters to argue below-ground living is a spiritually inert middle state, neither what a person ought to want nor what they actually want, making it distinct from ordinary sin or vice.
He explicitly separates below-ground living from mere screen time, insisting the underlying pattern is a discomfort with in-person life rather than any specific technology.
quotes: Below-ground living is a mode of life, a rhythm of existence that gravitates toward the ephemereal, the meaningless, and the elsewhere. It's a pattern whereby a person develops a discomfort with in-person life, opting whenever possible to substitute a digital alternative.

In below-ground living, digital devices are not tools, but furniture, the things that play the most active role in supporting day to day existence. Virtual communities become the "real" friends, who get access to personality while the family, coworkers, and classmates are left wondering, "What are they up to?

Household chores are not just a stodgy tradition. They're a way of acclimating a healthy young man to the pattern of responsibility, fulfillment, satisfaction: the immensely pleasurable sensation of being able to rest knowing that you've successfully completed the tasks you were given.
We overestimate the degree to which wins create confidence, and underestimate how being unafraid of failure creates it.

All the healthy and outgoing activities which we want him to avoid can be inhibited and nothing given in return, so that at last he may say, as one of my own patients said on his arrival down here, "I now see that I spent most of my life in doing neither what I ought nor what I liked.
This is below-ground living. It's neither how we ought to live, nor really the way we want to live. The glorious news is that it's not inevitable.
My friend and colleague Champ Thornton once shared with me a definition of manhood he has used with his (now grown) sons: "Manhood means moving toward people and problems in love and wisdom.
